description: Soil reaction in the arable layer. Central-Polish light-to-medium soils commonly acidify under ammonium-based N and residue removal; liming raises pH gradually. Crop effects should be small relative to fertilisation and liming, but legumes and brassicas can modestly increase Ca removal.

Set to 1 in the calendar year of a documented lime/CaO application; reset to 0 the following year. Used as a short-lived modifier for acidification response, clubroot risk and nutrient availability; the durable effect is represented by ph and acidificationCaO.

Annual net acidifying or neutralising balance, expressed as CaO equivalent. Positive values indicate net acidification; negative values indicate net liming. Inputs include N fertiliser form, residue export, legume N fixation, manure and lime. It updates ph through a soil-buffering function rather than changing pH directly.

Soil organic carbon in the VDLUFA humus-C convention, used for long-run soil-quality and N-supply dynamics. Perennial legumes, cover crops, farmyard manure and high-residue crops increase it; root crops, silage maize and intensive tillage reduce it.

Plant-available mineral N remaining after harvest, including unused fertiliser N, mineralised N and legume-derived N. It is available to the following crop and then reset after accounting for uptake, leaching, denitrification and immobilisation.

Microbial N demand generated by decomposing low-N residues, especially cereal straw, maize stover and mature grass residues. It is consumed during the following growing season and then reset; high values reduce early N availability and can increase fertiliser requirement.

Relative soil compaction state; negative values indicate loosening and positive values indicate compaction. Heavy harvest traffic, sugar-beet and potato operations, and wet-season field access increase it; deep-rooting crops, frost, drying and reduced traffic decrease it.

Relative arbuscular-mycorrhizal functionality, with 1 as neutral/reference. Non-host or strongly disruptive crops, especially oilseed rape and potato, reduce it; cereals, maize and legumes maintain or rebuild it. Used mainly as a response multiplier for phosphate-limited and root-health-sensitive crops.

Fraction of soil protected by living vegetation, stubble, mulch or cover crop during the main winter erosion/leaching period. Overwritten annually from the preceding crop, cover crop, stubble management and sowing date.

Take-all inoculum potential from infected cereal roots, stubble and grass weeds. It rises strongly after wheat, barley, rye and triticale, especially winter cereals, and declines rapidly when grass-free non-host breaks prevent root colonisation; AHDB notes that significant take-all is normally avoided after a non-susceptible crop. A 0.35 remaining fraction implies roughly 65% loss in the first host-free year, consistent with rapid decline of root/residue inoculum, while retaining a floor for grass weeds and volunteers.

Cereal Fusarium head blight and root/stem-base Fusarium pressure, driven by infected cereal residues and maize stover. It rises after cereals and grain/silage maize, particularly where residues remain near the surface, and declines as residues decompose. The decay value is an operational estimate for residue-borne inoculum under Polish tillage and climate conditions.

Eyespot inoculum from infected cereal stubble and stem bases. It increases after wheat, triticale, rye and barley, with winter cereals generally more exposed because infected residues carry into the next autumn; non-cereal breaks and residue decomposition reduce it. Decay reflects loss of infective stem-base residue over approximately 1-2 years.

Clubroot resting-spore pressure for Brassica crops. Resting spores are extremely persistent: reported half-lives are about 3.6-4.4 years, with viable spores potentially persisting for 15-20 years, although studies also report up to 90% decline within two host-free years. The registry uses 0.8 as a conservative annual remaining fraction, reflecting a multi-year half-life and the need to keep rapeseed out of infested fields for several years.

Sclerotinia sclerotiorum sclerotial pressure relevant to rapeseed, pulses and other broadleaf hosts. Sclerotia commonly remain viable for 3-10 years, with many reports of 4-5 years or longer; however, surface sclerotia can lose viability within about a year and non-host breaks of 2-3 years reduce inoculum. The registry uses 0.65 as a conservative central-Polish field average, between rapid surface decline and long persistence of buried sclerotia.

Rhizoctonia solani sensu lato pressure affecting potato, sugar beet, maize and seedlings of several crops. It persists on infested plant debris and sclerotia, with risk increased by short rotations, potato or beet following susceptible hosts, and cool/wet establishment. The decay value is an expert estimate for residue- and soil-borne inoculum decline under a non-host break.

Fusarium root-rot and wilt pressure specialised to grain and forage legumes. It accumulates after pea, faba bean, lupin and clover, especially under short legume intervals, and declines with non-legume breaks and residue decomposition. The decay value is an operational estimate; species-specific survival differs.

Colletotrichum-derived anthracnose pressure, primarily for lupin and other legumes. It builds with repeated lupin or susceptible legume cropping and infected residues/seed, then declines with non-host breaks and residue decomposition. The decay value is an expert estimate for use until a Polish host-specific survival dataset is available.

Aphanomyces euteiches root-rot pressure for pea and other legumes. Oospores can persist for many years in soil, so rotation alone gives only partial control; the registry uses 0.7 as a conservative annual remaining fraction, implying a multi-year decline rather than a one-year reset.

Heterodera schachtii cyst-nematode pressure for sugar beet and other Chenopodiaceae hosts. Cysts contain eggs that survive for years, but population decline without a host is substantial; the registry uses 0.6 as a conservative annual remaining fraction for central-Polish mineral soils. It should be raised sharply by beet and lowered by non-host breaks, resistant trap crops and appropriate soil-management practices.

Globodera rostochiensis/G. pallida cyst pressure for potato. Cysts and eggs can remain viable for 20 years or more, but natural population decline without potato is commonly around 30-35% per year; EPPO reports a first-year decline averaging 69% in sandy/peaty soils and 26% in loamy/clay soils. The registry uses 0.7 for light-to-medium central-Polish soils, a conservative value that avoids overstating the benefit of a one-year break.

Stem nematode (Ditylenchus dipsaci and related species) pressure, relevant to pulses, lupin, clover, potato and other hosts. It persists in soil, seed and plant residues, with host-specific populations; rotation with non-hosts reduces risk but does not eliminate it quickly. The decay value is an expert estimate for a non-host year.

Wireworm (Agriotes spp. and related elaterid larvae) pressure. It rises after grassy preceding crops, long-term grass/clover, weedy stubbles and high organic-matter conditions, and declines slowly under clean cultivated non-host rotations. The decay value is an expert estimate reflecting multi-year larval development rather than a single-season reset.

Western corn rootworm (Diabrotica virgifera virgifera) pressure. Eggs are laid in maize fields and larvae must find maize roots the following season; a non-maize year strongly suppresses the population, but extended-diapause and rotation-resistant behaviour can weaken this effect. The registry uses 0.1 remaining after one non-maize year, reflecting strong but not absolute rotation control.

Grass-weed pressure, including annual grasses and perennial grass weeds. It rises after cereals, maize, grass/clover and inadequate stubble control; broadleaf breaks, cover crops and targeted control reduce it. The decay value is an expert estimate for a year with effective non-host suppression; it should be modulated by herbicide efficacy, tillage and weed seed return.

Broadleaf-weed pressure, including difficult-to-control species and herbicide-resistance risk. It rises after broadleaf crops, incomplete control and seed return; cereals and grassy cover crops suppress many broadleaf weeds. The decay value is an expert estimate for a year with effective non-host suppression and should be modulated by herbicide programme and tillage.

Rapeseed volunteer pressure from harvest losses and dormant seed. It creates a Brassica host/green-bridge risk for clubroot and other rapeseed pathogens, and complicates following broadleaf crops. It declines as volunteers are controlled and seed dormancy is exhausted; the decay value is an expert estimate for one year of effective control.

Potato volunteer/tuber-regrowth pressure. Volunteers maintain potato cyst nematode, late blight, virus and Rhizoctonia risks and interfere with following crops. It declines rapidly with frost, cultivation, herbicide control and absence of host plants; the decay value is an expert estimate for one year of effective control.
